There is an hour in the morning when the world holds its breath. Not dawn exactly, but the moment after, when the light has arrived but the noise hasn't. I gravitate toward that quiet like a plant tilting toward a window. It feels stolen, as if the day hasn't noticed me yet and I can move through it unseen.

In that silence, small things become enormous. The click of a radiator. A bird landing on the fire escape, head tilting at a smudge on the glass. The soft scuff of my socks against the floorboards. Without the static, attention sharpens into something painful, and I realize how rarely I listen to my life.

I used to think freedom was loud—music, crowds, travel, confession. But more and more, freedom looks like an unremarkable Tuesday with no notifications and a kettle beginning to hum. It looks like choosing to sit still while the world accelerates. There is a strange power in not performing, in letting the hours pass without documentation.

Maybe that is the real luxury: not the absence of noise, but the ability to stop translating every moment into something useful. To let a thought arrive, linger, and leave without turning it into a plan. To be, for a little while, a creature instead of a brand.

So I pour the coffee, watch the steam curl, and let the morning be ordinary. The world will demand its noise soon enough. For now, I am simply here, and that is enough.
